idiom_name: impl Iterator / std::iter::successors / from_fn composed with map/filter/take
implementation_notes: Rust's lazy collection is the Iterator trait: the std documentation states iterators and iterator adapters are lazy and nothing happens until they are consumed, and the adapter library (map/filter/take/zip/scan) drives an unbounded or huge source one element at a time; std::iter::successors carries explicit state into an unbounded sequence and std::iter::from_fn builds one from a closure. Adapter chains are not memoized and are consumed by value, so repeated traversal needs a fresh iterator or a collected cache; memoized laziness for shared values is a separate primitive (LazyLock/OnceCell), and a plain Vec loop stays right for small hot data.
pitfalls: Iterator chains are inert until a terminal method runs: building a chain of adapters with no for/collect/sum does nothing (the compiler warns with unused_must_use on Iterator).

An iterator is consumed by value and next() takes &mut self, so a single iterator cannot be used twice or shared across threads; iterating twice requires an iterator factory and possibly a clone of the source.

Closures capturing owned state prolong that state's life for the whole chain (drop order of captured guards/buffers is the chain's drop order), and a chain holding a mutex guard across a by_ref() loop can deadlock.

variants.name: Async stream (futures::Stream / async-stream)
variants.idiom_name: impl Stream<Item = T> consumed by .next().await / try_next().await
variants.implementation_notes: Asynchronous lazy sequences are modelled by the futures-core Stream trait: next() is an async method resolving to Option<T>, consumed with while let Some(x) = stream.next().await or StreamExt adapters, and implemented by the async-stream crate's stream! macro, hand-written poll state machines, or combinations such as stream::unfold. Use it when each element depends on awaited I/O or a timer; cancellation is drop-based - dropping the stream drops the in-flight future at its next await point - and it replaces Iterator rather than composing with it (StreamExt::map/filter are async counterparts).
pitfalls: A hand-written Stream must store and wake the Waker: returning Poll::Pending without registering a waker produces a task that never wakes (silent stall).

Streams are driven by an executor - dropping the stream cancels at the next await point, but a resource held across an await is only released by the future's Drop, so leaking the future (mem::forget, cycles) hangs the producer.

StreamExt adapters are lazy like iterator adapters and equally inert without a terminal (for_each/collect/next), and some combinators (buffer_unordered) trade laziness for concurrency and reorder results.
